newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican troops in mass roundup of rebel suspects.
newsitem.headline: Mexican troops in mass roundup of rebel suspects.

text.p: Hundreds of police and troops arrested 11 men in a mountain Indian village in the biggest roundup yet of suspected guerrillas in southern Mexico, officials said on Friday.

The arrests on Wednesday and Thursday in San Agustin Loxicha in Oaxaca state include the mayor and other top municipal officials. State justice officials say they may be founding members of the rebel Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR).

Five Loxicha citizens were arrested on terrorism charges on Thursday, Oaxaca Attorney General Roberto Pedro Martinez Ortiz told reporters. The day before, six others were seized in a raid that human rights groups said involved at least 800 soldiers carrying out house-to-house searches.

"It's the biggest operation so far against members of the EPR," Martinez spokesman Noel Cruz Matias said. He said there were another 14 arrest warrants out for Loxicha citizens and troops and police continued to comb the remote area some 50 miles (80 km) south of the state capital, Oaxaca.

The EPR, which emerged publicly in June, carried out a series of raids on military and police targets in late August in Oaxaca and several other states. The state government accused the Loxicha citizens of taking part in the most bloody gunbattle near the Pacific resort of Huatulco, an attack on Aug. 28 in which nine people were killed.

Progress in hunting down the EPR across southern Mexico has been patchy but Martinez said the latest captures may include guerrilla ringleaders. San Agustin Loxicha's mayor, Agustin Luna Valecia, "is one of the leaders of the guerrilla group," he said, accusing him of recruiting rebels and leading them to a mountaintop training camp for combat practice.

Luna Valencia has also been charged with using his truck to drive rebels to Huatulco for the Aug. 28 attack. Police were led to Loxicha, where residents staged mass protests against the army in early September, after a guerrilla found dead at the scene of the attack was identified as the village treasurer.
Human rights groups in contact with the village said soldiers carried out house-to-house searches without proper warrants, but state officials said the operation was carried out in full legality.
The discovery of a village rife with rebel suspects may reflect a nucleus of support for the EPR, which the government has denounced as a terrorist organisation with no social base.
